CAGR.long:
CAGR — compound annual growth rate — collapses a multi-year return into the single steady annual rate that would produce the same start-to-end result. Ten thousand becoming twenty thousand over five years gives a CAGR of about 14.9%, the fifth root of the ratio minus one. It only ever compares two dates.

What it rewards is the ratio of final capital to starting capital, nothing else. It has no memory of the path in between — a smooth climb and a path that fell hard mid-way then recovered can post an identical CAGR, because the calculation never looks past the two endpoints.

That blindness is also the standard gaming move: choose start and end dates that flatter the number. Beginning the clock just after a bad stretch, or ending it just before one, changes the reported figure without changing anything about the underlying strategy.

Where people get fooled: two equity curves with the same CAGR can carry completely different risk, one earned with a shallow drawdown and one with a brutal one. Quoting CAGR alone hides which kind is being sold, which is why it belongs next to a drawdown figure and a stated window, never alone.
CAGR.usage: Used to compare compounding rates across strategies or periods on a common footing, never as a stand-in for how the return was actually earned.

Total return.long:
Total return is the change in an investment's value over a period including everything paid out along the way — dividends, coupons, distributions — not just the change in price. A share that fell 5% in price but paid a 6% dividend has a positive total return despite a falling chart.

It rewards completeness: nothing about the investor's actual cash outcome is left out. What it does not reward is disclosure of terms — whether the figure is gross or net of fees and tax, and whether income was assumed reinvested, all change the number without changing the label attached to it.

The standard gaming move is silence about which version is being quoted. A gross, reinvested total return over a favourable window looks materially better than the net, un-reinvested figure that actually lands in an account, and both get called simply "total return."

Where people get fooled: a price chart is compared against a quoted total-return figure as though they measure the same thing, and the gap between them gets attributed to skill or to a flaw in the chart, when it is usually just the dividends the chart never plotted.
Total return.usage: Read alongside its stated basis — gross or net, reinvested or not — before comparing it against any other figure, since two total returns computed on different conventions are not the same measurement.

MAR ratio.long:
The MAR ratio divides compound annual growth rate by the maximum drawdown suffered getting there, giving a single number for return earned per unit of worst pain endured. A strategy compounding at 15% a year through a 20% maximum drawdown scores a MAR of 0.75.

It rewards a favourable ratio of growth to the single worst peak-to-trough loss in the sample. It ignores everything about that drawdown except its depth — how long it lasted, how often smaller ones recurred, and whether the sample period happened to contain the strategy's actual worst case at all.

The gaming move follows directly: a short backtest window that never lived through a real stress event reports a small denominator and an inflated MAR, flattering exactly the strategies that have not yet been tested by anything difficult.

Where people get fooled: a high MAR ratio reads as "efficient," but the ratio only knows about the drawdown the sample happened to contain. A strategy with a genuinely fat left tail can carry an excellent MAR right up until the sample finally includes the event that was always waiting in it.
MAR ratio.usage: Used to compare compounding efficiency across strategies, always checked against the length and content of the sample the drawdown was measured over.

Ulcer index.long:
The ulcer index measures both the depth and the duration of drawdowns by squaring the percentage decline below the prior peak at every point in a series, averaging, and taking the root — a strategy that lingers underwater scores worse than one that dips hard but recovers fast, even at the same maximum depth.

That is the feature it rewards over a plain maximum-drawdown figure: two strategies can post an identical worst dip while one spends a week below its peak and the other spends two years. The ulcer index tells them apart; a single max-drawdown number cannot.

It still depends entirely on the sample it is computed over, and it says nothing about the frequency of trades or the source of the drawdowns, only their shape once they happen.

Where people get fooled: a strategy report leads with maximum drawdown and stops there, so two strategies with the same headline figure look equally uncomfortable to hold, when one recovered in days and the other left an account underwater for most of its history — the difference the ulcer index exists to expose.
Ulcer index.usage: Used alongside maximum drawdown to distinguish a quick, sharp dip from a slow, grinding one that a headline drawdown figure alone cannot tell apart.

Time under water.long:
Time under water is the length of a drawdown — the stretch between an equity high and the point the curve finally reclaims it — measured in trading days, weeks, or months rather than in percentage terms. It answers a different question to drawdown depth: not how far it fell, but how long the account had to wait.

It rewards fast recovery and penalises strategies that grind sideways below a prior peak for long stretches, even when the depth of that drawdown was unremarkable. A shallow but prolonged drawdown can carry more time under water than a sharp, brief one that recovered within weeks.

On its own it says nothing about depth, which is why it is normally read next to the drawdown figure rather than instead of it — the two describe different axes of the same discomfort.

Where people get fooled: an equity curve chart that ends at a new high looks like a success story regardless of the path, but a curve that spent most of its history below a previous peak was mostly in drawdown the whole time it was being shown — the final tick up is the only part the chart draws attention to.
Time under water.usage: Read alongside drawdown depth, since a strategy can look tame on maximum drawdown and still spend most of its life recovering from it.

Omega ratio.long:
The omega ratio weighs the full return distribution against a chosen threshold, dividing the probability-weighted size of gains above it by the probability-weighted size of losses below it. Unlike Sharpe, it uses every observation rather than collapsing the distribution to a mean and a variance, so it can pick up skew that a symmetric measure misses.

That sensitivity is also its weak point: the ratio's value depends entirely on where the threshold is set, and there is no single correct choice. A strategy that looks strong against a zero threshold can look weak against a threshold set at the risk-free rate, with nothing about the underlying returns having changed.

Because the threshold is a free parameter, it can be chosen after the fact to flatter whichever strategy is being reported, which is the standard gaming move with this metric specifically.

Where people get fooled: an omega ratio is quoted as though it were a single fixed property of a strategy, when it is a function with a hidden input. Two honest reports of the same strategy at two different thresholds can rank it in opposite order against a competitor.
Omega ratio.usage: Compared only across strategies computed at the same stated threshold, since the ratio's ranking of two strategies can flip when the threshold does.

Tail ratio.long:
The tail ratio compares the size of extreme gains to the size of extreme losses, typically the return at the 95th percentile divided by the absolute return at the 5th percentile. It describes the shape of the outer edges of a return distribution rather than its centre, which mean and standard deviation both ignore.

It rewards a distribution whose big up-moves outsize its big down-moves, and it is blind to frequency — a strategy can have a favourable tail ratio while losing on most individual trades, because the ratio only ever looks at the extremes, not how often each side occurs.

The number is fragile in a short sample: percentile estimates at the far ends of a distribution are set by a handful of observations, so one unusually large day can move the ratio substantially without reflecting anything structural about the strategy.

Where people get fooled: a strong tail ratio from a few hundred trades is often really a description of the single best and single worst day in the sample, dressed up as a distributional property — the next few hundred trades can move it a long way just by chance.
Tail ratio.usage: Read as a description of a limited sample's extremes rather than a stable property, and treated with more caution the shorter the trade history behind it.

Skew.long:
Skew is the third statistical moment of a return distribution, describing its asymmetry. Positive skew means frequent small losses and occasional large gains — the shape typical of trend-following. Negative skew means frequent small gains and occasional large losses — the shape typical of option-selling and many mean-reversion approaches.

Skew rewards nothing on its own; it is descriptive, not a performance score. What it does is warn about the character of the losses a strategy is exposed to, independent of its average return or its volatility — two strategies with identical mean and standard deviation can have opposite skew and completely different worst-case behaviour.

Negative skew is the more dangerous shape to be unaware of, because the strategies that carry it typically look calm for long stretches, collecting small regular gains right up until the rare loss that erases many of them at once.

Where people get fooled: a smooth, steadily rising equity curve is read as low risk, when a smooth curve made of many small wins is frequently the visible signature of negative skew — the risk is real, it is simply concentrated in the days the curve has not shown yet.
Skew.usage: Checked before trusting a smooth equity curve, since negatively skewed strategies routinely look calmest right before the rare loss that defines their risk.

Kurtosis.long:
Kurtosis is the fourth statistical moment, measuring how heavy a distribution's tails are relative to a normal curve — how often extreme observations occur, in either direction, beyond what a bell curve would predict. It is a separate question from skew, which is about direction, not frequency of extremes.

High kurtosis rewards nothing directly; it is a warning label. It says that outlier days — in either direction — are more common than a normal-distribution model assumes, so any risk figure built on that assumption, from standard deviation to a naive Value at Risk, is calibrated against a calmer world than the one generating the data.

Financial return series routinely show far higher kurtosis than a normal distribution, which is one reason volatility clusters and crashes both happen more often, and more suddenly, than symmetric statistics predict.

Where people get fooled: a risk model quietly built on a normal-distribution assumption produces confident-looking numbers precisely where kurtosis makes them least trustworthy — the extreme event that breaks an account is, by construction, the kind of observation the model assumed away.
Kurtosis.usage: Used as a check on whether a risk figure derived from standard deviation or a normal-distribution assumption can be trusted for the tails, not just the middle.

Rolling returns.long:
Rolling returns recompute a return over a fixed window — twelve months, say — at every point in a series rather than once, producing a whole distribution of holding-period outcomes instead of a single figure. Plotted over time, they show how an investor's result would have varied depending on exactly when they started.

They reward a fuller picture of consistency than one headline return can give, showing whether good performance was concentrated in a few periods or spread evenly across the sample.

What they do not do is add independent evidence in proportion to how many windows are shown, because adjacent windows overlap almost entirely — a twelve-month window starting in January and one starting in February share eleven months of the same underlying data.

Where people get fooled: forty overlapping rolling windows drawn from six years of data look like forty separate track records, when they are the same six years counted forty times over. Any statistic on the spread of rolling returns needs a correction for that overlap, or it reports far more confidence than the data supports.
Rolling returns.usage: Used to see how a strategy's outcome varied by starting date, with the overlap between windows kept in mind before treating the spread as independent evidence.

Equity curve.long:
The equity curve is the plot of account or strategy value over time — the most basic and most persuasive chart in trading, because it compresses an entire history into one visual shape. Everything else, from drawdown to CAGR, is a number extracted from this curve.

It rewards nothing by itself; it is a chart, not a metric, and its persuasiveness is exactly the problem. A rising line reads as success regardless of the path taken to get there, the leverage used, or the tail risk quietly building beneath a run of small gains.

Presentation choices change its effect without changing the underlying numbers: a log scale compresses large moves and flatters volatility, a cropped window hides whatever came before it, and a chart with costs left out shows a strategy that was never actually tradeable.

Where people get fooled: a smooth-looking curve is read as a safe strategy, when smoothness is a property of the chart's scale and window as much as of the strategy — the curve that eventually breaks often looked identically smooth right up until it did.
Equity curve.usage: Read alongside its scale, window, and whether costs are included, since the same underlying trades can be plotted to look calmer or wilder depending on those choices alone.

Underwater curve.long:
The underwater curve plots drawdown as a percentage below the prior equity peak at every point in time, sitting at or below zero throughout. Where the equity curve shows the highs, the underwater curve shows nothing but the troughs — every drawdown's depth and duration made visible at once.

It rewards honesty about the parts of a track record the equity curve tends to compress: a chart that looks smooth on a rising line can reveal, once inverted this way, that the strategy spent long stretches meaningfully below its own high point.

It adds nothing the equity curve doesn't technically contain, but it puts the uncomfortable part in the foreground instead of the background, which changes what a reader actually notices.

Where people get fooled: a report that shows only the equity curve and quotes a single maximum-drawdown figure can still hide a strategy that spent most of its history underwater — the underwater curve is the chart most likely to be left out of a pitch, precisely because it is the one that would show it plainly.
Underwater curve.usage: Checked whenever a maximum-drawdown figure is quoted alone, since the underwater curve shows how often and how long the account actually spent below its peak.

Annualisation.long:
Annualisation scales a shorter-period statistic — a daily Sharpe ratio, a monthly return, a weekly volatility figure — up to an annual number, usually by multiplying return by the number of periods in a year and volatility by the square root of that number. It gives figures measured on different frequencies a common footing for comparison.

The square-root-of-time scaling for volatility rewards a specific, quiet assumption: that returns are independent from one period to the next. Where that assumption fails — and volatility clustering and autocorrelation mean it usually does to some degree — the annualised figure is systematically distorted, not just approximate.

The gaming move is choosing which short period to annualise. A strategy's best month, scaled up by twelve, produces a headline annual number built entirely from one period of good luck.

Where people get fooled: an annualised figure is treated as a forecast of a full year's likely result, when it is arithmetic performed on a much shorter window — annualising a short period multiplies its noise right alongside its signal, and a lucky month makes an equally lucky year on paper.
Annualisation.usage: Read as a scaled description of the period actually measured, not as a projection, and checked for which period was chosen before comparing it to anything else.

Value at Risk.long:
Value at Risk states a loss threshold for a given confidence level and horizon — a one-day 95% VaR of $10,000 means that, historically or under a model, losses have exceeded $10,000 on about 5% of days. It is a single quotable number, which is exactly why it is used so widely in risk reporting.

Its documented failure mode is built into its own definition: VaR is a threshold, not a worst case. It says nothing whatsoever about how large a loss can be once that threshold is breached — the 5% of days beyond the line could exceed it by a small margin or by the entire account, and VaR cannot distinguish between the two.

Firms have cleared their stated VaR limits comfortably right up until the day they didn't, because the metric was never designed to describe that day — only to mark the edge of the ordinary range.

Where people get fooled: VaR is read as a ceiling on possible loss, when it is only a boundary that gets crossed a known fraction of the time by an unknown amount — the entire point of the tail beyond it is what the number does not measure.
Value at Risk.usage: Read strictly as a stated-confidence threshold, never as a ceiling on the worst possible loss, and always paired with a measure of what happens beyond it.

Expected shortfall.long:
Expected shortfall, also called conditional VaR, is the average loss in the tail beyond the Value at Risk threshold — where VaR marks the edge of the ordinary range, expected shortfall describes the size of what typically happens once that edge is crossed.

It rewards a fuller picture of tail risk than VaR alone, and it has a mathematical property VaR lacks: it behaves consistently when portfolios are combined, which is why regulators have shifted toward it. It still depends on the same confidence level VaR does, and the answer changes with that choice.

Its remaining weakness is data: estimating the average size of a rare event from a historical sample that may contain few or none of them is itself a noisy exercise, however coherent the maths downstream of that estimate are.

Where people get fooled: expected shortfall computed from a backtest with no real crisis in it is describing a tail the sample never actually contained — it inherits VaR's blind spot one level further in, dressed in a number that looks more sophisticated for having done so.
Expected shortfall.usage: Used alongside Value at Risk to size the average loss beyond the threshold, with the honest caveat that the underlying tail data is often thin.

Stress testing.long:
Stress testing applies a specific, named adverse scenario — a historical crash, a flash crash, a rate shock — to a portfolio or strategy to see what happens, rather than relying only on whatever the historical return sample happened to contain. It is a deliberate attempt to look at conditions the backtest data may be missing.

It rewards direct confrontation with plausible bad outcomes that a smooth historical sample would otherwise hide, forcing a concrete answer to "what happens if this specific thing occurs" rather than a vague sense of safety.

Its limit is that it only tests the scenarios someone chose to write down. Every stress test is built by imagining a version of the last crisis, and the next one, definitionally, tends not to look exactly like the last.

Where people get fooled: passing a list of stress scenarios feels like proof of robustness, but the list was authored by a person recalling the past — the genuinely dangerous scenario is, by construction, the one nobody thought to include, which no amount of passing the existing list can rule out.
Stress testing.usage: Run against named historical or hypothetical shocks to see a portfolio's behaviour outside its own sample, understood as covering only the scenarios chosen, not every possible one.

Scenario analysis.long:
Scenario analysis explores how a portfolio or strategy would perform under a range of hypothetical future states — different growth environments, rate paths, or market regimes — rather than testing a single named historical shock the way stress testing does. It is a structured way to think through "what if" without needing the event to have already happened.

It rewards breadth of imagination about the future and forces assumptions into the open where they can be examined, rather than leaving them implicit in a single point forecast.

What it cannot supply is the probability of each scenario, and that number is usually a guess presented with a table's authority — the scenarios themselves are chosen by a person, and people tend to choose scenarios consistent with what they already believe is most likely.

Where people get fooled: a table of scenarios with precise-looking figures attached implies a precision the underlying probabilities never had. The output looks quantitative because the arithmetic inside each scenario is exact, even though which scenarios made the table, and how likely each was judged, were not.
Scenario analysis.usage: Used to pressure-test a position or plan against a spread of plausible futures, with the probability attached to each scenario treated as a stated assumption, not a measured fact.

Benchmark-relative.long:
A benchmark-relative figure measures performance as the gap to a chosen benchmark — an index, a peer group, a risk-free rate — over the same period, rather than as a standalone number. It answers a sharper question than absolute return alone: not just what happened, but what happened beyond what was already available for free.

It rewards separating genuine skill from market exposure — a strategy that simply holds a leveraged version of an index will show a large absolute return and, once compared properly, very little benchmark-relative return once the extra risk is accounted for.

What it does not automatically do is adjust for the risk taken to generate the gap. A benchmark-relative return achieved with materially higher volatility than the benchmark is not the same achievement as the same gap earned at similar or lower volatility.

Where people get fooled: outperforming a benchmark by running twice its volatility gets described as skill, when unadjusted for risk it may simply be leverage — a benchmark-relative figure quoted without its accompanying risk comparison hides exactly which one is being shown.
Benchmark-relative.usage: Read together with a risk comparison to the same benchmark, since an unadjusted gap can be produced by leverage as easily as by genuine edge.

Cherry-picked period.long:
A cherry-picked period is a start and end date chosen, consciously or not, because the window between them makes a result look better than a longer or differently placed window would. It is the mechanism behind most inflated CAGR and total return figures, since both are entirely determined by their two endpoints.

It rewards nothing; it is a selection artefact, not a property of a strategy. What makes it effective is that the chosen window looks like ordinary data once shown — nothing about a cherry-picked chart announces that a worse-looking stretch was cropped from before or after it.

The same effect applies to backtests: a start date placed just after a strategy's worst historical stretch, or an end date placed just before a foreseeable reversal, produces numbers that describe the window, not the strategy.

Where people get fooled: a chart that appears to "start working" from a particular date onward is treated as evidence the underlying idea improved, when it is frequently evidence the window itself was chosen after seeing what came before it — the improvement lives in the selection, not in the strategy.
Cherry-picked period.usage: Checked by asking who chose the start and end dates and why, before trusting any return figure computed over a specific window.

Survivor track record.long:
A survivor track record is a performance history that is visible precisely because the fund, manager, or strategy behind it survived long enough to keep reporting — the failed peers that would have pulled the average down have already closed, stopped publishing, and dropped out of view.

It rewards nothing directly; it describes an artefact of which records happen to still exist. Any average computed across a set of visible track records is, by construction, an average of the survivors, and survival itself is correlated with having had a good run.

The effect compounds across an industry: databases of fund performance systematically under-represent closed funds, and the gap between the reported average and the true average across everyone who ever started grows with how aggressively failures are removed from view.

Where people get fooled: browsing a set of long-running, visible track records and averaging their returns overstates what a new entrant should expect, because the sample excludes everyone who did not make it this far — a track record's continued existence is itself evidence it beat the odds of not existing.
Survivor track record.usage: Read with the awareness that any visible set of long track records has already been filtered by survival, before using it to estimate what a new strategy should expect.

Fixed dollar risk.long:
Fixed dollar risk sizes every trade to risk the same absolute amount of money — say $200 — regardless of account size, computed as that fixed amount divided by the distance from entry to stop. It is the simplest sizing method and the easiest to audit from a trade log.

It rewards consistency and simplicity: every trade carries a known, comparable dollar risk, which makes expectancy easy to track over time without adjusting for a moving account balance.

What it does not do is scale with the account. As equity grows, a fixed dollar amount becomes a shrinking percentage of the balance, which is mild and self-correcting; as equity falls, the same fixed amount becomes a growing percentage of what remains, which is the opposite of what a losing stretch calls for.

Where people get fooled: fixed dollar risk feels conservative because the number on the ticket never changes, but as a drawdown deepens, that unchanging number consumes an ever larger share of the remaining account — the method that felt cautious at the start becomes aggressive exactly when the account can least afford it.
Fixed dollar risk.usage: Used for its simplicity and auditability, with the trade-off understood: the percentage of the account it represents rises automatically during a losing stretch unless adjusted manually.

Percent volatility sizing.long:
Percent volatility sizing sets position size so that a fixed percentage of account equity is put at risk based on the instrument's recent volatility, commonly using ATR — a more volatile instrument gets a smaller position, a calmer one a larger position, so each trade risks a comparable dollar amount of expected movement.

It rewards putting different instruments on a common footing: without it, a volatile commodity and a quiet index would carry very different real risk at the same nominal position size. Normalising by volatility corrects for that directly.

What it does not do is distinguish risk from opportunity. Volatility rising can mean a genuine trend is accelerating just as much as it can mean conditions are simply choppier, and the formula sizes down in both cases identically.

Where people get fooled: sizing down as volatility rises can mean cutting position size right as a real trend is picking up steam — the method manages the variance of the outcome, not the odds of being right, and treating the two as the same thing leads to systematically smaller bets exactly when a trend is finally moving.
Percent volatility sizing.usage: Used to normalise risk across instruments of different volatility, kept distinct from any judgement about whether rising volatility signals opportunity or danger.

Fixed ratio.long:
Fixed ratio money management, developed by Ryan Jones, increases position size in fixed steps as trading profit accumulates: a trader holds one contract until cumulative profit clears a chosen threshold, called the delta, then adds a second, and so on — with each additional contract requiring the same delta to clear before the next one is added.

It rewards fast early compounding compared with a strategy that only scales as a percentage of a growing account, because size increases in whole steps rather than smoothly, front-loading growth while the account is still small.

The delta itself is a free parameter with no unique correct value, chosen by the person designing the scheme — which makes it a second thing to fit alongside the underlying strategy's own parameters, with its own capacity to be tuned to a particular equity curve.

Where people get fooled: a fixed ratio scheme tested on the same equity curve that inspired its delta will look unusually smooth, because the delta was implicitly chosen to fit a path that had already happened — the smoothness is partly a property of the fit, not of the scheme applied to a genuinely unknown future.
Fixed ratio.usage: Applied with the delta parameter treated as a variable that can itself be overfit to a specific backtest, not as a fixed, objectively correct setting.

Pyramiding.long:
Pyramiding adds to a position that has already moved favourably, buying more at new, higher prices in an uptrend or shorting more at new, lower prices in a downtrend, so the total position grows while the trade is working.

It rewards a trade that has already partly proven itself, putting more capital behind an idea after the market has agreed with it rather than committing full size at the uncertain entry. It also raises the average entry price toward the current, less favourable level, and increases total capital at risk from a higher base.

Each addition is effectively a new trade layered onto an existing one, with its own entry, its own implied risk, and its own contribution to how a reversal from the current, higher price affects the whole position — not a simple extension of the original decision.

Where people get fooled: pyramiding feels like "letting profits run," but a reversal after several additions can erase the gains of the earliest ones entirely — a trader tracking only the blended average entry price often does not notice how much of the position's risk now sits at prices far above where the trade began.
Pyramiding.usage: Treated as a series of separate sizing decisions, each with its own risk contribution, rather than as a single trade that simply grew.

Scaling out rules.long:
Scaling out rules are a predefined plan for closing a position in stages rather than all at once — for example, a third of the position at one times the initial risk, a third at two times, and the remainder left to run under its own management.

They reward reduced variance in the outcome and less pressure on any single exit decision, since no one moment determines the whole result. What they do not do is offer something for nothing: the portion closed early gives up whatever it would have earned had it stayed on, in any scenario where price kept moving favourably afterward.

Where the splits are set changes the shape of the resulting distribution — an aggressive early split behaves more like a fixed-target strategy, a light early split behaves more like a pure trend-following one, and the rules should match which of those is actually wanted.

Where people get fooled: scaling out is often sold as a way to "have it both ways," but selling half a position at an early target genuinely halves the exposure exactly when a trend trade's edge, if it has one, is typically still ahead of it rather than behind it.
Scaling out rules.usage: Set in advance as a specific split and set of trigger levels, not decided in the moment, since a plan improvised mid-trade tends to track the trader's comfort rather than the market.

Risk parity across strategies.long:
Risk parity across strategies allocates capital so each strategy in a combined portfolio contributes roughly equal risk, rather than equal dollar allocation — typically by weighting inversely to each strategy's volatility, so a jumpy strategy gets a smaller allocation and a steady one a larger allocation.

It rewards preventing one high-volatility strategy from dominating the combined portfolio's swings simply because it happened to receive the same dollar allocation as calmer ones. The volatility and correlation estimates it depends on are themselves noisy and change over time, and they tend to shift fastest, and least favourably, during genuine stress periods.

Crucially, equalising risk contribution says nothing about whether any of the underlying strategies has a real edge in the first place — it only balances how much each one can move the combined account.

Where people get fooled: risk parity is mistaken for a source of return rather than a way of blending existing sources. Combining several strategies with no real expectancy, in perfectly balanced risk proportions, still produces a portfolio with no expectancy — only smoother variance on the way to it.
Risk parity across strategies.usage: Applied to strategies that have already been checked for genuine, independent expectancy, since balancing risk contribution across strategies with none only smooths the path to a flat outcome.

Anti-martingale in practice.long:
Anti-martingale sizing increases position size after wins and decreases it after losses — the opposite of a martingale, which doubles into losses. In practice this is usually implemented as raising risk percentage after a winning streak and cutting it after a losing one.

It rewards, in principle, sizing that tracks whatever is currently working rather than compounding into what is currently failing, and it avoids the ruin mechanism built into doubling down. What it assumes, though, is that a recent run of results reflects a real change in edge rather than ordinary variance.

A short winning streak from a strategy with genuine edge and a short winning streak from a strategy with none look statistically identical in the short run — regression to the mean applies to both equally, regardless of which produced the streak.

Where people get fooled: increasing size after a hot streak is a bet that the streak reflects skill rather than luck, made at precisely the moment the evidence for that distinction is weakest — the streak that triggered the larger size is often the same streak about to mean-revert.
Anti-martingale in practice.usage: Applied cautiously, since sizing up after a streak assumes the streak is informative about a real change in edge, which a short run of results cannot reliably confirm.

Grid trading.long:
Grid trading places a ladder of buy and sell orders at fixed price intervals around a reference price, adding to the position at each level reached regardless of direction, and profiting from oscillation within the range — often with no stop loss, relying on price eventually returning inside the grid.

It rewards a small, steady stream of gains for as long as price stays range-bound, which is what makes it attractive on a short backtest. What it rarely defines is a maximum loss: each new grid level adds exposure at a worse price if the move keeps going.

The arithmetic is stark. A grid that doubles size at each level — one lot, two, four, eight — reaches 1,024 lots after ten levels, and the next tick's loss scales the same way; a sustained trend through enough levels does not merely dent the account, it can consume it.

Where people get fooled: a grid strategy's equity curve in a ranging market looks like free, steady income, when that income is the premium for selling insurance against a genuine trend — insurance never priced, because the size a trend eventually demands is invisible until it arrives.
Grid trading.usage: Understood as a structural concentrator of risk into trending moves, with the position size at any given level of adverse movement worked out and compared to account capital before it is used.

Averaging in vs averaging down.long:
Averaging in is adding to a position at predetermined levels according to a plan written before the trade began, sized within a total risk cap set in advance. Averaging down is adding to a position that has moved against the original entry, most often decided in the moment, usually to lower the average cost basis rather than to follow a pre-set plan.

The two are structurally different decisions that can look identical after the fact. Averaging in, done properly, is a sizing plan the trader committed to before knowing which way price would move. Averaging down, done reactively, reopens a decision — the original stop — that had already been made.

What distinguishes them is timing, not intention as remembered afterward: whether the additional levels and the total risk were written down before the position was underway, or invented once the loss was already in progress.

Where people get fooled: averaging down on every loser and calling it averaging in only ever gets tested by whether the plan predates the loss. On the trade log the two look the same; only one of them was risk management, and only the timestamp on the original plan can tell them apart.
Averaging in vs averaging down.usage: Distinguished strictly by whether the additional entries and their total risk were written down before the trade began, not by how disciplined the decision felt at the time.

Maximum position count.long:
A maximum position count rule caps the number of concurrent open positions, or the number of positions in correlated instruments, that a trader or system will hold at once, as a simple guard against unintentionally large aggregate exposure.

It rewards a hard ceiling on how many separate bets can be running simultaneously, which is useful when correlation between them is otherwise easy to overlook. What it depends on for that protection to actually work is an accurate view of which positions are genuinely correlated, and correlation between markets is itself unstable, typically rising fastest during the stress events the cap exists to survive.

A count-based cap treats every position as equally independent regardless of what actually drives it, which is a simplification that holds only as long as the positions really are unrelated.

Where people get fooled: five positions across five different tickers look diversified by the count alone, but if they share one underlying macro driver, a rule that only counts tickers has capped nothing that actually mattered when that driver moves.
Maximum position count.usage: Set with an eye on what actually correlates the candidate positions, not just their ticker count, since a count-based cap only limits risk where the positions are genuinely independent.

Risk per setup type.long:
Risk per setup type assigns different risk budgets to different categories of trade setup — more risk to setups judged higher-conviction, less to those judged lower-conviction — instead of applying a uniform risk amount to every trade regardless of category.

It rewards, in principle, sizing that tracks genuine differences in expected edge across setup types, if those differences are actually measured. What it requires to work as intended is enough tracked history per category to know, with real sample size, which setups actually carry more expectancy — without that, "conviction" is a feeling rather than a measurement.

Absent a tracked, per-category expectancy, differential sizing tends to concentrate risk on whichever setup type felt most convincing recently, and recent performance is a poor stand-in for a setup's actual long-run edge.

Where people get fooled: allocating more risk to the setup that "feels" strongest is frequently allocating more risk to whichever category happened to win most recently — without a tracked expectancy per setup type, risk per setup type is discretion dressed in a system's language.
Risk per setup type.usage: Applied only once each setup category has a tracked sample size large enough to estimate its own expectancy separately, rather than sized off which category feels most convincing lately.

Capital preservation mode.long:
Capital preservation mode is a rule set that reduces risk — smaller position size, lower trade frequency, or both — once a defined drawdown threshold has been crossed, intended to protect the remaining account and slow the compounding of further losses during a bad stretch.

The recovery arithmetic it responds to is asymmetric and worth stating plainly: a 20% drawdown needs a 25% gain to get back to even, while a 50% drawdown needs a 100% gain, so cutting size after a loss reduces how much further behind the next bad trade can put the account.

The same move locks in a smaller base right before a possible recovery, so if the drawdown was ordinary variance rather than a broken edge, reduced size compounds more slowly through the very recovery that would have restored the account fastest.

Where people get fooled: cutting size after a drawdown feels obviously prudent, but it is itself a bet — that the drawdown reflects a broken edge rather than normal variance — and getting that bet wrong by cutting into a genuine recovery costs, in compounding terms, roughly what failing to cut before a real breakdown costs.
Capital preservation mode.usage: Triggered by a threshold set in advance, understood as a bet on whether the drawdown reflects a genuine change in edge, which the threshold itself cannot determine.

Exit strategy.long:
An exit strategy is the plan for how a position will be closed — a price target, a stop level, a time limit, or a set of discretionary conditions — decided before the trade is entered rather than worked out once it is already running.

It rewards clarity that survives contact with a live position: a plan written in advance is a commitment made before the outcome could bias it, while a plan assembled after entry is shaped by whatever the position has already done, which is exactly the input an exit rule is meant to be independent of.

Many trading plans are detailed on entry criteria and vague on this half of the trade, treating the exit as something that will become obvious once the moment arrives.

Where people get fooled: "I'll know it when I see it" sounds like flexibility, but the moment it describes always arrives already coloured by the running profit or loss — a target that moves because the trade is up, or a stop that gets excused because the trade is down, was never really the plan, it was the position talking.
Exit strategy.usage: Written down before entry, alongside the entry criteria, so the exit is a decision made in advance rather than a reaction to the trade's own progress.

Stop placement logic.long:
Stop placement logic is the reasoning behind where a stop-loss sits, as distinct from simply having a stop at all. Common approaches place it beyond a structural chart level, at a multiple of a volatility measure, at a fixed dollar or percentage distance, or at a time limit rather than a price level.

A stop placed by structural or volatility logic is designed to sit at the point where the original trade thesis is actually disproven, so being stopped out carries information about the idea itself. A stop placed purely by "how much I'm willing to lose" can sit well inside the instrument's normal daily noise, unrelated to whether the thesis still holds.

The two approaches can produce an identical dollar distance from entry while meaning entirely different things when the stop is hit.

Where people get fooled: two stops at the same distance from entry can carry opposite information — one sits just past a level that genuinely invalidates the setup, the other sits in the middle of ordinary chop — and only the logic behind the placement, never the dollar figure alone, tells the two apart.
Stop placement logic.usage: Chosen based on what actually disproves the trade thesis, with the dollar risk following from that level rather than the level being chosen to fit a preferred dollar risk.

Invalidation.long:
Invalidation is the specific, pre-defined price or condition at which the reason a trade was taken is no longer true — distinct from the trade simply being unprofitable at the moment. It is the level a stop is, ideally, placed around.

It rewards a clean separation between two very different situations that otherwise blur together: the market proving the original thesis wrong, and the market merely moving against an open position temporarily. Without a written invalidation point, every losing trade sits ambiguously between those two readings.

A thesis with no stated invalidation cannot really be tested, because there is no price at which it would have been shown to be incorrect — it can always be reinterpreted as still valid, just delayed.

Where people get fooled: that ambiguity is exactly the gap where a plan gets abandoned mid-trade for reasons that sound like fresh analysis but are really the open position influencing the read. A pre-written invalidation level closes that gap before the trade starts, not after it is already uncomfortable.
Invalidation.usage: Defined before entry as the specific condition that disproves the trade thesis, kept separate from the emotional discomfort of an open loss.

Structural stop.long:
A structural stop is placed based on a level in the chart's own structure — beyond a recent swing high or low, or past a support or resistance level — rather than at an arbitrary fixed distance from entry, tying the stop to the point where the trade's thesis would actually be disproven.

It rewards a stop that means something: being hit generally coincides with the structure the trade depended on genuinely breaking, rather than with an arbitrary distance being reached. The trade-off is that structural levels often sit further from entry than a fixed-distance stop, which lowers the position size available for a given dollar risk.

That means the order of operations runs from the chart to the position size, not the reverse: the structural level sets the stop distance, and the stop distance sets how large the position can be for the chosen risk.

Where people get fooled: sizing the position first and placing the stop wherever fits a pre-decided dollar risk inverts this logic entirely — a stop chosen to fit the position size, rather than the reverse, is not structural no matter which chart level it happens to land near.
Structural stop.usage: Set from the chart first, with position size then derived from the resulting stop distance rather than the stop distance being fitted to a pre-chosen position size.

Volatility stop.long:
A volatility stop sets the distance from entry to stop as a multiple of a volatility measure, most commonly ATR, so the stop automatically widens in choppier conditions and tightens in calmer ones rather than sitting at one fixed distance across every regime.

It rewards adapting to an instrument's recent behaviour instead of applying the same number to a quiet range day and a fast trending one. A volatility measure built from recent history can lag a genuine shift in regime, arriving late exactly when conditions are changing fastest — and the multiple applied to it, whether one, two, or three times ATR, is a free choice with no uniquely correct value.

Because that multiplier is a parameter like any other, it can be adjusted after the fact to whichever setting produced the best-looking backtest, which quietly reintroduces the arbitrariness the volatility measure was meant to remove.

Where people get fooled: a volatility stop feels objective because it comes out of a formula, but the multiplier behind it was still chosen by a person — testing several multiples until one looks best on historical data is parameter fitting wearing the appearance of a rule.
Volatility stop.usage: Set with a stated, fixed multiplier decided in advance, rather than adjusted after seeing which multiple happens to produce the best-looking backtest.

Stop too tight.long:
A stop is too tight when it sits inside an instrument's normal noise range, so ordinary price movement — not genuine invalidation of the trade thesis — is what triggers it. The trade can be stopped out repeatedly for reasons that have nothing to do with whether the original idea was right.

A tighter stop rewards a smaller dollar risk per trade, which allows a larger position size for the same total risk. That benefit is partly or fully cancelled if the tighter distance sits inside the instrument's routine range, because the larger position then gets stopped out more often before it has a real chance to reach target.

Whether a stop is too tight is a property of the instrument's typical movement, not of the trader's comfort with the dollar amount at risk — the two are frequently confused for one another.

Where people get fooled: a string of small, quick losses gets read as the market being wrong, rather than as the stop sitting somewhere the instrument routinely visits on an ordinary day. The fix is checking the stop distance against the instrument's typical range before the next trade, not after the tenth stop-out.
Stop too tight.usage: Checked against the instrument's typical intraday or intra-swing range before entry, rather than diagnosed only after several consecutive stop-outs.

Target selection.long:
Target selection is the method for choosing where a position will be closed for profit — a fixed multiple of the initial risk, a prior structural level, a volatility-based projection, or a fully discretionary read of the moment.

A target set from structure or a stated risk-to-reward multiple ties the exit to something observable and fixed before the trade begins. A target set by feel tends to move as the trade develops — further away when the position is running well, closer when the trader is anxious about giving profit back — which converts a fixed plan into a running negotiation with the open position.

That negotiation is invisible from inside the trade, since every individual adjustment can feel like a reasonable response to new information rather than a pattern of moving the goalposts.

Where people get fooled: extending a target because "it's really running" and pulling it in because "I don't want to give it back" are the same underlying behaviour wearing two different justifications — a target that changes with the running profit and loss was never really a target, it was a mood tracked in price.
Target selection.usage: Fixed before entry as a specific level or ratio, with any mid-trade adjustment checked against whether it follows the original plan or simply follows the current profit and loss.

Partial exit.long:
A partial exit closes part of a position while leaving the remainder open, most often used to lock in some realised profit while retaining exposure to further favourable movement, and to reduce the psychological weight of an all-or-nothing decision.

It rewards a genuine reduction in the variance of the outcome — locking in something removes the risk of the entire trade reversing to a loss — but it is not a free improvement. The portion closed early gives up whatever it would have earned had it remained open, in every scenario where price continued to move favourably afterward, which is exactly the scenario a trend trade is usually taken hoping for.

It is, mathematically, a blend of two different outcomes rather than an enhancement of one, and the blend point is chosen by where the split is set.

Where people get fooled: a partial exit is described as eliminating regret, but it only redistributes it — sell too early and the regret shows up on the winners that kept running afterward; sell too late and it shows up on the ones that reversed. The trade-off does not disappear, it just changes which side of it stings.
Partial exit.usage: Applied as a stated split decided before the trade, not adjusted mid-trade to fit whichever outcome would minimise regret in hindsight.

Runner management.long:
Runner management covers the decisions made about the portion of a position left open after a partial exit — how its stop trails, whether it carries a further target, and how long it is allowed to stay open, distinct from the decisions already made about the part that was closed.

A wide trailing stop on the runner rewards capturing more of a genuinely extended move, giving the position room to breathe through ordinary pullbacks that a tighter stop would exit on. That same width gives back more of the runner's open profit if the move stalls rather than continuing, since the stop has to be far enough away to tolerate normal noise as well as a real reversal.

There is no trailing method that captures large moves without also surrendering a meaningful share of open profit on the moves that merely stall.

Where people get fooled: watching a runner give back half its open profit feels like a management failure, but that give-back is close to unavoidable with any trailing stop loose enough to stay in for a genuinely large move — the same slack that lets it capture the big one lets an ordinary pullback take a bite too.
Runner management.usage: Managed with a trailing method chosen in advance for how much give-back it accepts in exchange for staying in a genuinely extended move.

Moving a stop.long:
Moving a stop is adjusting a stop-loss level after a position is already open. It can mean tightening it — moving it to breakeven once a trade has proven itself, for example — or widening it, giving a losing trade more room than the original plan allowed.

Tightening toward breakeven, if it was part of the original plan, buys comfort at a real cost: it exits some genuine winners early on the pullback that triggers the tightened level, in exchange for guaranteeing more trades end flat rather than as a loss. Widening a stop because the original level was hit or is close to being hit removes the one predefined point where the thesis was declared wrong, turning a bounded loss into an open-ended one.

Both are the same mechanical action — changing a price on an order — but they carry opposite consequences for the trade's risk.

Where people get fooled: "giving the trade more room" and "moving the goalposts" are the same action described by two different moods. The tell is whether the new level was decided before the trade went underwater or invented once it already had.
Moving a stop.usage: Restricted to adjustments that were part of the original plan, such as moving to breakeven on a pre-set trigger, rather than widened in response to the position moving against the original stop.

Trade thesis.long:
A trade thesis is the specific, written reason a trade was taken — what has to be true about the market for it to work — as distinct from the entry signal alone, which can trigger without any explanation of why it should matter.

A genuine thesis is falsifiable: it specifies conditions under which it would be wrong, before the outcome is known. "I think it goes up" fails that test, because nothing about it can be disproven in advance — any outcome can be made to fit it afterward.

Writing the thesis down before entry is what makes the later review of the trade meaningful, since a plan recorded before the outcome is known cannot be quietly reshaped by the outcome once it arrives.

Where people get fooled: a trade taken on a signal with no accompanying thesis gets a thesis invented afterward to match whatever happened — a winner gets "I knew it would break out," a loser gets "the market just did something unusual" — and neither retrospective story can inform the next trade, because neither existed before the result was known.
Trade thesis.usage: Written before entry as a specific, falsifiable statement, so a later review can check the outcome against the original reasoning rather than a reasoning invented to match it.

Holding period.long:
A holding period is the length of time a position is intended to be held, ideally set in advance by the trade's timeframe, the setup that generated it, or a specific catalyst it is waiting on — rather than by how the position happens to be performing at any given moment.

A holding period fixed in advance gives an objective point at which to reassess the trade on its own terms. One that stretches when a trade is winning and shrinks when it is losing is not really a plan; it tracks profit and loss rather than the reasoning the trade was based on.

That asymmetry — patient with winners, impatient with losers, or the reverse — is a well-documented behavioural pattern, not a coincidence, and it shows up in how long positions are actually held far more reliably than in what traders say their rule is.

Where people get fooled: "I'm holding because it's working" and "I'm holding because I don't want to realise the loss" look identical from the outside. A holding period set in advance is the only way to tell, after the fact, whether a trade was held for a reason or held out of hope.
Holding period.usage: Set by the setup's own timeframe before entry, checked against actual holding times afterward to see whether winners and losers were treated by the same rule.

Adding to winners.long:
Adding to winners means increasing position size in a trade that has already moved favourably — a form of pyramiding — as distinct from adding to a losing position, which is a different decision with a different risk profile entirely.

Each addition raises the average entry price toward the current market level, lengthening the potential right tail of the trade if the move continues, while also raising the drawdown volatility of the combined position — a given adverse move against the larger, later size does more dollar damage than the identical move would do against the smaller original size, because the position is now bigger and closer to the recent peak.

Neither effect is automatically good or bad; both are real and simultaneous, and the net result depends on how the additions are sized and stopped.

Where people get fooled: "letting winners run" and "adding to winners" are treated as the same idea, but adding is a fresh risk decision with its own stop and its own effect on account variance — a position comfortably sized at entry may not stay comfortably sized after two additions, even though each one looked reasonable when it was made.
Adding to winners.usage: Sized as a series of distinct additions each with its own risk, checked against the account's total exposure rather than assumed to be a costless extension of the original trade.

Exit on time.long:
Exiting on time means closing a position because a pre-defined time limit was reached — a session close, a fixed number of bars, an option's expiry, or a scheduled event deadline — rather than because price hit a target or a stop.

It rewards removing exposure to conditions outside the intended window, such as overnight gap risk or a thesis that has run past the period it was actually about, and it prevents a position from being held indefinitely simply because neither the target nor the stop has been reached yet.

The same rule can also close a position moments before the move it was taken for actually arrives, since a fixed time limit has no way to distinguish a thesis that failed from one that is simply running late.

Where people get fooled: a strategy that exits on time and shows a smooth equity curve may just be avoiding the volatility that happens outside its chosen window — that avoided volatility includes both the losses it dodged and the gains it never collected, and a smooth curve alone does not say which side dominates.
Exit on time.usage: Set as a fixed limit tied to the setup's own timeframe, distinguished clearly from a stop or target so the reason for any given exit is recorded accurately.

Reversal vs exit.long:
A reversal closes a position and opens the opposite one in the same action; a plain exit closes it and stops there. A reversal bundles two judgements into one decision: that the current trade is wrong, and that the opposite trade is now right.

An exit alone rewards a clean stopping point, leaving what to do next, if anything, as a separate question asked afresh. A reversal can capture a genuine turn efficiently when both halves of that bundled judgement are correct, but the second half rarely gets the independent scrutiny a fresh trade would normally receive, since it inherits the urgency of having just been wrong on the first one.

The new position in a reversal is entered under the emotional charge of the trade that just failed, which is not the same condition under which it would have been generated as a standalone idea.

Where people get fooled: flipping from long to short right after a stop-out feels like decisive risk management, but it is frequently frustration wearing a strategy's clothes — sized and entered in reaction to the last trade rather than through the process that produces a genuinely fresh one.
Reversal vs exit.usage: Treated as two separate decisions even when executed together — the exit judged on its own merits, and the new position required to clear the same entry bar as any other fresh trade.

Post-exit review.long:
A post-exit review checks a closed trade against its original written thesis, entry plan, and exit plan — asking whether the plan was followed, not simply whether the trade made money, since those are two different questions with two different answers.

It rewards judging process ahead of outcome: a trade can be reviewed as well executed despite losing, if the plan was followed and the loss was the plan working as designed, and reviewed as poorly executed despite winning, if the plan was abandoned along the way and the win was simply lucky.

A review process only has value if it covers trades evenly rather than selectively, since a biased sample of reviews teaches lessons that do not generalise to the trades left unexamined.

Where people get fooled: reviewing only losing trades, or only reviewing when there happens to be time, biases the sample toward whichever outcomes felt uncomfortable enough to revisit — a review process that mainly shows up after losses ends up studying variance, not the plan itself.
Post-exit review.usage: Applied consistently to wins and losses alike, judged against the original written plan rather than against the profit or loss the trade produced.

Slippage on exit.long:
Slippage on exit is the gap between the intended exit price and the price a position is actually filled at when closing — distinct from slippage on entry, and frequently larger, because exits are often triggered by the same fast-moving conditions that make fills worse in the first place, such as a stop hit during a sharp move or a gap through a level.

A market order rewards a guaranteed exit but accepts whatever fill quality the moment offers, which can be materially worse during exactly the volatile conditions that most often trigger stops. A limit order protects the intended price but risks not filling at all while price runs straight through it.

Neither choice removes the trade-off; it only decides which side of it — certainty of execution or certainty of price — gets sacrificed when conditions turn fast.

Where people get fooled: a backtest that fills every stop at the exact stop price is quietly assuming zero slippage on precisely the trades most likely to have it — the fast, gappy moves that trigger stops in the first place are the same conditions in which real fills lag the intended price the most.
Slippage on exit.usage: Modelled explicitly in any backtest rather than assumed away, since the trades most likely to trigger a stop are also the ones most likely to fill worse than the stop price.

One trade at a time.long:
One trade at a time is a rule limiting exposure to a single open position, or a single active decision, rather than running several simultaneously — a simplicity constraint on how much is happening in the account at once.

It rewards keeping attention on one plan at a time and reduces the chance that stress from managing one trade bleeds into the sizing or management of another running alongside it. What it also does is cap opportunity by count alone: a genuinely independent setup that appears while a position is already open gets skipped regardless of its own individual merit.

The rule is often adopted to fix a problem that is really about correlation rather than count — several positions that all move together because they share one underlying driver, mistaken for genuine diversification simply because they carry different ticker symbols.

Where people get fooled: a strict one-position rule adopted to solve correlated overexposure ends up rejecting a genuinely uncorrelated opportunity as well, since it caps by number of trades rather than by what actually drives the risk in each one.
One trade at a time.usage: Used as a discipline constraint on attention and correlated exposure, with the underlying cause of any prior overexposure checked first to confirm it was correlation and not simply count.
